lesson.title: Ratios and Proportions: Scaling the World Up and Down
lesson.summary: A ratio compares two quantities, and a proportion sets two equal ratios side by side so you can solve for an unknown value, a technique behind map scales, recipes, unit prices, and many other ACT word problems.
lesson.body:
A ratio is a comparison between two quantities, written as a to b, a colon between a and b, or the fraction a/b. It looks like a fraction and often behaves like one, since a ratio such as 6 to 8 simplifies the same way 6/8 does, down to 3 to 4. But a ratio is doing something a plain fraction is not always doing: it is comparing two separate quantities, like miles to gallons, or boys to girls in a classroom, rather than describing a single part of a single whole. Keeping that distinction in mind helps you set up word problems correctly, because the order you list the quantities in matters and must stay consistent.

A proportion is simply a statement that two ratios are equal, and it is one of the most useful tools on the ACT because it lets you find an unknown quantity from a known relationship. If 2 inches on a map represents 15 real miles, that relationship, 2/15, stays constant no matter how many inches you are measuring. So if two cities are 7 inches apart on the map, you can set up the proportion 2/15 = 7/x, where x is the unknown real distance. To solve, cross multiply, meaning you multiply the numerator of one side by the denominator of the other: 2 times x equals 15 times 7, so 2x = 105, and dividing both sides by 2 gives x = 52.5 miles. Cross multiplication works because it is really just multiplying both sides of the equation by both denominators at once to clear the fractions, the same legal move you will use constantly once you start solving equations more formally.

You can always check a proportion answer by plugging it back in and comparing decimals: 2 divided by 15 is about 0.1333, and 7 divided by 52.5 is also about 0.1333, so the ratios genuinely match. That kind of check, converting both sides to decimals and comparing, is a fast way to catch a setup mistake before you commit to an answer choice.

The most common way students lose points on ratio and proportion problems is not the arithmetic, it is the setup. If the problem says '3 red marbles for every 5 blue marbles,' the ratio must stay red over blue, or blue over red, but it has to be the same order on both sides of any proportion you write. Flipping one side and not the other gives an answer that is the reciprocal of the correct one, a small mistake with a big consequence. Reading carefully and labeling each number as you write the ratio, red = 3, blue = 5, is the single best habit for avoiding this trap.
